{{Short description|Ruled surface over the projective line}}
In mathematics, a '''Hirzebruch surface''' is a [[ruled surface]] over the [[projective line]]. They were studied by {{harvs|txt|first=Friedrich|last=Hirzebruch|year=1951|authorlink=Friedrich Hirzebruch}}.

==Definition==
The Hirzebruch surface <math>\Sigma_n</math> is the <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math>-bundle (a [[projective bundle]]) over the projective line <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math>, associated to the [[Sheaf (mathematics)|sheaf]]<math display="block">\mathcal{O}\oplus \mathcal{O}(-n).</math>The notation here means: <math>\mathcal{O}(n)</math> is the {{mvar|n}}-th tensor power of the [[Serre twist sheaf]] <math>\mathcal{O}(1)</math>, the [[invertible sheaf]] or [[line bundle]] with associated [[Cartier divisor]] a single point. The surface <math>\Sigma_0</math> is isomorphic to <math>\mathbb P^1\times \mathbb P^1</math>; and <math>\Sigma_1</math> is isomorphic to the [[projective plane]] <math>\mathbb P^2</math> blown up at a point, so it is not minimal.

=== GIT quotient ===
One method for constructing the Hirzebruch surface is by using a [[GIT quotient]]:<ref name=":0">{{cite arXiv | last=Manetti | first=Marco | date=2005-07-14|title=Lectures on deformations of complex manifolds | eprint=math/0507286 }}</ref>{{rp|21}} <math display="block">\Sigma_n = (\Complex^2-\{0\})\times (\Complex^2-\{0\})/(\Complex^*\times\Complex^*)</math> where the action of <math>\Complex^*\times\Complex^*</math> is given by <math display="block">(\lambda, \mu)\cdot(l_0,l_1,t_0,t_1) = (\lambda l_0, \lambda l_1, \mu t_0,\lambda^{-n}\mu t_1)\ .</math> This action can be interpreted as the action of <math>\lambda</math> on the first two factors comes from the action of <math>\Complex^*</math> on <math>\Complex^2 - \{0\}</math> defining <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math>, and the second action is a combination of the construction of a direct sum of line bundles on <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math> and their projectivization. For the direct sum <math>\mathcal{O}\oplus \mathcal{O}(-n)</math> this can be given by the quotient variety<ref name=":0" />{{rp|24}}<math display="block">\mathcal{O}\oplus \mathcal{O}(-n) = (\Complex^2-\{0\})\times \Complex^2/\Complex^*</math>where the action of <math>\Complex^*</math> is given by<math display="block">\lambda \cdot (l_0,l_1,t_0,t_1) = (\lambda l_0, \lambda l_1,\lambda^0 t_0=t_0, \lambda^{-n} t_1)</math>Then, the projectivization <math>\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{O}\oplus\mathcal{O}(-n))</math> is given by another <math>\Complex^*</math>-action<ref name=":0" />{{rp|22}} sending an [[equivalence class]] <math>[l_0,l_1,t_0,t_1] \in\mathcal{O}\oplus\mathcal{O}(-n)</math> to<math display="block">\mu \cdot [l_0,l_1,t_0,t_1] = [l_0,l_1,\mu t_0,\mu t_1]</math>Combining these two actions gives the original quotient up top.

=== Transition maps ===
One way to construct this <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math>-bundle is by using transition functions. Since affine vector bundles are necessarily trivial, over the charts <math>U_0,U_1</math> of  <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math> defined by <math>x_i \neq 0 </math> there is the local model of the bundle<math display="block">U_i\times \mathbb{P}^1</math>Then, the transition maps, induced from the transition maps of <math>\mathcal{O}\oplus \mathcal{O}(-n)</math> give the map<math display="block">U_0\times\mathbb{P}^1|_{U_1} \to U_1\times\mathbb{P}^1|_{U_0}</math>sending<math display="block">(X_0, [y_0:y_1]) \mapsto (X_1, [y_0:x_0^n y_1])</math>where <math>X_i</math> is the affine coordinate function on <math>U_i</math>.<ref>{{Cite web | title=Algebraic Geometry|url=https://dn710302.ca.archive.org/0/items/gathmann-notes-2002-version/Gathmann%20notes%20%282002%20version%29.pdf | last=Gathmann|first=Andreas | date=|website= Fachbereich Mathematik - TU Kaiserslautern |archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=}}</ref>

== Properties ==

=== Projective rank 2 bundles over P<sup>1</sup> ===
Note that by [[Birkhoff–Grothendieck theorem|Grothendieck's theorem]], for any rank 2 vector bundle <math>E</math> on <math>\mathbb P^1</math> there are numbers <math>a,b \in \mathbb Z</math> such that<math display="block">E \cong \mathcal{O}(a)\oplus \mathcal{O}(b).</math>As taking the projective bundle is invariant under tensoring by a line bundle,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Section 27.20 (02NB): Twisting by invertible sheaves and relative Proj—The Stacks project|url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02NB| website=stacks.math.columbia.edu|access-date=2020-05-23}}</ref> the ruled surface associated to <math>E = \mathcal O(a) \oplus \mathcal O(b)</math> is the Hirzebruch surface <math>\Sigma_{b-a}</math> since this bundle can be tensored by <math>\mathcal{O}(-a)</math>.
==== Isomorphisms of Hirzebruch surfaces ====
In particular, the above observation gives an isomorphism between <math>\Sigma_n</math> and <math>\Sigma_{-n}</math> since there is the isomorphism vector bundles<math display="block">\mathcal{O}(n)\otimes(\mathcal{O} \oplus \mathcal{O}(-n)) \cong \mathcal{O}(n) \oplus \mathcal{O}</math>

=== Analysis of associated symmetric algebra ===

Recall that projective bundles can be constructed using [[Relative Proj]], which is formed from the graded sheaf of algebras<math display="block">\bigoplus_{i=0}^\infty \operatorname{Sym}^i(\mathcal{O}\oplus \mathcal{O}(-n))</math>The first few symmetric modules are special since there is a non-trivial anti-symmetric <math>\operatorname{Alt}^2</math>-module <math>\mathcal{O}\otimes \mathcal{O}(-n)</math>. These sheaves are summarized in the table<math display="block">\begin{align}
\operatorname{Sym}^0(\mathcal{O}\oplus \mathcal{O}(-n)) &= \mathcal{O} \\
\operatorname{Sym}^1(\mathcal{O}\oplus \mathcal{O}(-n)) &= \mathcal{O} \oplus \mathcal{O}(-n) \\
\operatorname{Sym}^2(\mathcal{O}\oplus \mathcal{O}(-n)) &= \mathcal{O} \oplus \mathcal{O}(-2n)
\end{align}</math>For <math>i > 2</math> the symmetric sheaves are given by<math display="block">\begin{align}
\operatorname{Sym}^k(\mathcal{O}\oplus \mathcal{O}(-n)) &=
\bigoplus_{i=0}^k \mathcal{O}^{\otimes (n-i)}\otimes \mathcal{O}(-in)
\\
&\cong \mathcal{O}\oplus \mathcal{O}(-n) \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathcal{O}(-kn)
\end{align}</math>

=== Intersection theory ===
Hirzebruch surfaces for {{math|''n'' > 0}} have a special [[rational curve]] {{math|''C''}} on them: The surface is the projective bundle of <math>\mathcal{O}(-n)</math> and the curve {{math|''C''}} is the [[zero section]]. This curve has [[Intersection theory|self-intersection number]] {{math|−''n''}}, and is the only irreducible curve with negative self intersection number. The only irreducible curves with zero self intersection number are the fibers of the Hirzebruch surface (considered as a [[fiber bundle]] over <math>\mathbb P^1</math>). The [[Picard group]] is generated by the curve {{math|''C''}} and one of the fibers, and these generators have intersection [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]]<math display="block">\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -n \end{bmatrix} , </math>so the [[bilinear form]] is two dimensional unimodular, and is even or odd depending on whether {{mvar|n}} is even or odd.
The Hirzebruch surface {{math|Σ<sub>''n''</sub>}} ({{math|''n'' > 1}}) blown up at a point on the special curve {{math|''C''}} is isomorphic to {{math|Σ<sub>''n''+1</sub>}} blown up at a point not on the special curve.

=== Toric variety ===
The Hirzebruch surface <math>\Sigma_n</math> can be given an [[Group action|action]] of the [[complex torus]] <math>T = \mathbb{C}^*\times \mathbb{C}^*</math>, with one <math>\mathbb{C}^*</math> acting on the base <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math> with two fixed axis points, and the other <math>\mathbb{C}^*</math> acting on the fibers of the vector bundle <math display="inline">\mathcal{O}\oplus \mathcal{O}(-n)</math>, specifically on the first line bundle component, and hence on the projective bundle. This produces an open orbit of ''T'', making <math>\Sigma_n</math> a [[toric variety]]. Its associated fan partitions the standard lattice <math>\mathbb{Z}^2</math> into four cones (each corresponding to a coordinate chart), separated by the rays along the four vectors:<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Cox |first1=David A. |title=Toric varieties |last2=Little |first2=John B. |last3=Schenck |first3=Henry K. |author-link=David A. Cox |author-link2=John B. Little (mathematician) |author-link3=Hal Schenck |date=2011 |publisher=American mathematical society |isbn=978-0-8218-4819-7 |series=Graduate studies in mathematics |location=Providence (R.I.) |pages=112}}</ref> <blockquote><math>(1,0), (0,1), (0,-1), (-1,n).</math></blockquote>All the theory above generalizes to arbitrary toric varieties, including the construction of the variety as a quotient and by coordinate charts, as well as the explicit intersection theory. 

Any smooth toric surface except <math>\mathbb{P}^2</math> can be constructed by repeatedly [[blowing up]] a Hirzebruch surface at ''T''-fixed points.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Cox |first1=David A. |title=Toric varieties |last2=Little |first2=John B. |last3=Schenck |first3=Henry K. |date=2011 |publisher=American mathematical society |isbn=978-0-8218-4819-7 |series=Graduate studies in mathematics |location=Providence (R.I.) |pages=496}}</ref>
